doc.title: Derrick Gardner interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 9, 2013

title: Does race matter for young jazz musicians today?
summary: Gardner says no; jazz is now international, with African roots and African-American origins.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Here’s a hard question, and I thought of it because I just attended a research presentation by a student here and she wrote a paper, she was doing research basically on women in © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -9-

jazz, and partially race, but she was mostly focusing on gender. But in your opinion, in today’s scene, does it make a difference if a young musician trying to get into the business is African-American or Caucasian or Asian? Does it make a difference these days?
No. No, I don’t think it makes a difference. You’re speaking specifically to jazz?

No. I believe that everybody, no matter where they come from, has something to contribute. And jazz has been given to the world as America’s contribution to the world of music you know. And African-Americans are the people that gave this music, that offered this music through the borders of America to the world. And so now it has become an international music. And Asians are exposed to it, Europeans are exposed to it, Australians are exposed to it you know, Africans are exposed to it — it being a big difference between being African and African-American. It’s two different cultures. There are many transcendental things that are similar between our two cultures, but still it’s two different cultures. And so when jazz is being exposed to Africans, those inherent African things that are similar can come out but there is still some differences, like [scats] the ride cymbal beat is right in tune with the six-eight feel that you hear in African music all the time, but it had slowed down. [rushes] one-two-three-four-five-six [scats drums]. You’re gonna shuffle [scats]. Now you can break it down like that, then this is African [scats], you know, that upbeat [scats]. And those are the things that are similar, and even the bending of those pitches, you know? That wasn’t done in European music. That wasn’t done in American music until it came up from the music that was brought about during the time of slavery and how those field hollars and work songs, how those bent pitches started to work themselves into the fabric of American music, you know. And so a lot of different things that I think — I think I’m kind of going off on a tangent here — but there are many different — because jazz is now an American music — sorry — jazz is now an international music, those people who are being exposed to it are now able to contribute to it you know. And you don’t have to be a non-African-American in order to contribute to it. I don’t believe that at all.
